title: The Power of Preteaching
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane argues that math teachers with occasional small-group intervention time default to using it as remediation -- filling gaps in content students have just struggled with in class. He proposes flipping that default: use pull-out time to preteach the concepts students are about to encounter, so they walk into the whole-class lesson already primed for success. Kane frames this as complementary to, not a replacement for, remediation, and connects it to a broader philosophy that motivation follows success -- students who feel capable at the start of a lesson are more likely to stay engaged through its harder parts. Because pull-out groups are usually small, preteaching sessions can move at a pace and level of individualized attention that a whole-class lesson cannot, letting the teacher build genuine early confidence rather than repeatedly patching the same gaps after the fact.
points: Kane's core reframe: most small-group intervention time defaults to remediation of content already taught, but preteaching upcoming content lets students arrive at the whole-class lesson already primed to succeed.
The proposal rests on a motivation argument -- early success predicts sustained engagement -- rather than purely a content-coverage argument.
Because pull-out groups are small, preteaching sessions can move at an individualized pace that a whole-class lesson structurally cannot replicate.
The approach is pitched as a complement to remediation, not a wholesale replacement for it, in schools where intervention time is limited.
quotes: I have a bit of time each week where I can pull students and work with them individually or in small groups. What should I do with that time?
There's a really ineffective form of intervention that plays catch-up. Maybe it's homework help after school, or support with independent work in class.
in many cases, one of the factors why they aren't learning in class is that they feel unsuccessful. They try to pay attention and class doesn't make sense so they tune out.
Preteaching can take a student who often doesn't pay much attention in class, who often feels unsuccessful, and help them see that they can learn, that effort in class pays off.

I've had students who are often distracted in class — constant side conversations, not paying attention, etc. But I have the chance to pull them for some one-on-one work, I preview what we're going to learn the next day, and suddenly they're answering questions and engaged.
The goal of preteaching is to help students build better learning habits in class. Putting extra work into key skills that play a big role in the future can pay big dividends down the road.
